title: Well-baby assessment: key checks and early-life red flags

steps.tx: A **well-baby assessment** checks growth, feeding, development and examination in the first weeks and months of life. Each visit should screen for conditions that are easy to miss, such as **developmental dysplasia of the hip**, congenital hypothyroidism and anaemia. Careful history, including birth presentation and family history, guides which examinations are needed.

steps.tx: Neonatal jaundice needs urgent attention when the bilirubin is very high or the infant looks unwell. Haemolytic disease, such as **ABO incompatibility** with a positive direct antiglobulin test, requires **urgent phototherapy** and serial bilirubin checks. Lethargy, poor feeding or jaundice to the knees in an older newborn suggests bilirubin neurotoxicity and needs immediate admission.

steps.tx: **Vitamin K prophylaxis** prevents late vitamin K deficiency bleeding, because newborns have low stores and limited gut flora. Parents may decline. The clinician should explain the bleeding risk, offer the option again, and document an **informed refusal**. Child protection referral is not appropriate for a competent, well parent who has made an informed choice.

steps.tx: Anaemia in infancy is most often caused by **iron deficiency**. Exclusively breastfed infants are at risk after about four to six months, because breast milk has low iron and stores run out. Iron-rich complementary foods and **oral iron supplementation** treat and prevent it. Check haemoglobin, MCV and ferritin to confirm the diagnosis before treating.

steps.tx: Safe sleep counselling lowers the risk of **sudden infant death** and suffocation. Infants should sleep **supine** on a firm, bare surface, with no soft bedding, pillows or bumpers. Bed-sharing is hazardous, especially when a tired parent may fall asleep while feeding in an adult bed. Room-sharing without bed-sharing is the advised alternative.

steps.tx: Congenital hypothyroidism presents with poor feeding, constipation, prolonged jaundice and a large fontanelle. A raised TSH with low free T4 on repeat testing confirms the diagnosis. **Levothyroxine** must start without delay, because thyroid hormone is needed for brain development and untreated disease causes irreversible intellectual impairment.
